releases.title: July 2026
releases.summary: A batch of new features, fixes, and under-the-hood hardening — all landed on main, all covered by tests, all on your machine. All ten new features are live in Settings today: adjustable AI cleanup, voice editing, a self-learning dictionary, rich local formatting, spoken-filename @-mentions for code editors, agent-CLI cleanup, and output targets that route a dictation to a file, a macOS Shortcut, or a webhook.

entries.headline: Say a filename, get an @-mention — hands-free file references in Cursor & Windsurf
entries.body: Speak a file the way you'd read it aloud — “main dot t s”, “at main”, “index dot j s x” — and OpenWhisp writes @main.ts / @main / @index.jsx so your editor's own file autocomplete pops up. It's a pure, offline text transform, and it's deliberately timid: only clear filename forms are rewritten, so ordinary speech (“I ate lunch”, “the main point”, “at noon”) is never touched.

howTo.summary: Turn it on once in Settings, then say the filename in Cursor or Windsurf; the “dot <ext>” or leading “at” cue becomes an @-mention.
steps: Turn it on: Settings › Cleanup › Formatting › “Enable file tagging in code editors” (off by default).

Dictate into Cursor or Windsurf and say the filename the way you'd read it: the name, the word “dot”, then the extension spelled out letter-by-letter (“main dot t s”) or as a whole word (“main dot swift”).
Or lead with “at” for a bare mention: “at main” → @main.
The @-mention lands in your editor and its file autocomplete disambiguates the rest.
say: “open main dot t s and fix it” → open @main.ts and fix it
howTo.note: Works in Cursor and Windsurf when the Settings toggle is on — OpenWhisp only converts spoken filenames while one of those editors is frontmost, so ordinary dictation everywhere else (chat, docs) is never touched. Off by default. An optional AX read of the open workspace to auto-pick the exact extension is still a stretch goal.

entries.headline: Use your Claude or Codex CLI as the AI cleanup engine
entries.body: Pipe your dictation through a coding-agent CLI you already have installed — claude, codex, or any command that reads stdin — and reuse the subscription you already pay for as the cleanup model. No separate API key, no extra service: it's the inverse of Agent Bridge, consuming an agent as the refine engine.

howTo.summary: Point OpenWhisp at a local agent CLI (e.g. claude -p) and it cleans up each dictation using your own subscription.
steps: Open Settings › Cleanup › AI Model and set Provider to “Agent CLI (Claude / Codex)”.
Pick a preset — Claude Code (claude -p) or Codex (codex exec) — or choose Custom and enter any command that reads stdin and writes the cleaned text to stdout.

Turn on “Improve every dictation automatically” below (or use Refine on demand). OpenWhisp feeds your transcript to the CLI on stdin — never on the command line, so nothing you say can be interpreted as a command — and uses its output as the refined text.
If the CLI is missing, errors, times out, or returns nothing, OpenWhisp keeps your original words — you never lose a dictation.
howTo.note: Reuses your locally-installed CLI and its own login — no API key needed here. Where your text goes depends on which CLI you pick (a cloud coding agent, or a fully local model).

entries.headline: Send your dictation straight into a macOS Shortcut
entries.body: Route the final transcript into any Shortcut you've built — add it to Things or Reminders, append to a note, fire a webhook, run AppleScript. One OS-level integration reaches the whole Shortcuts ecosystem, and if the shortcut can't run, your text falls back to normal insertion so nothing is ever lost.

howTo.summary: Pick a Shortcut in Settings; OpenWhisp runs it with your transcript as the input.
steps: Build a Shortcut in Shortcuts.app that starts with “Receive input” (text) and does whatever you want with it.
Open Settings › Output › Output target and choose Shortcut, then pick your Shortcut from the list (or type its name and Refresh).
Dictate as usual — OpenWhisp runs `shortcuts run <name>` with your transcript on stdin and hands the text off.
howTo.note: Live now. Runs on the final transcript only (live-typing always goes to the focused app). On any error or timeout it fails open to normal insertion, so your words are never lost.

entries.headline: Adjustable AI cleanup, from a light touch to a full polish
entries.body: Pick how much the AI reshapes your words — None, Low, Medium, or High — and OpenWhisp always keeps your raw transcript so you can revert to exactly what you said in one click.

howTo.summary: Choose a cleanup level in Settings; revert to your exact words anytime.
steps: Open Settings › Cleanup › Automatic Cleanup and pick a level on the dial: None (verbatim, no AI pass), Low (fixes caps, punctuation, spelling), Medium (also removes fillers and lightly rephrases), or High (also resolves spoken self-corrections like “3, no wait, 4” → “4”).
Dictate as usual — the level you chose is applied automatically to each final transcript. None skips the AI entirely.
In Settings › Privacy › History, click the revert (↺) button next to any entry the AI reshaped to swap the cleaned text back to your raw words — the originals are copied to your clipboard.
howTo.note: Live now. The dial is the single source of truth for AI cleanup — the old on/off “Improve every dictation” toggle (tray + onboarding) now just reflects it. Higher levels trade literal fidelity for polish; the revert button appears only when the AI actually changed your words. Revert currently covers the standard preview and insert-at-end dictation modes (not the live-streaming per-chunk mode, which pastes as it types). It lives in History and, right after a dictation lands, in the post-dictation overlay — a one-tap “Revert to original” pill that swaps the cleaned text back to your raw words in place when it safely can, and otherwise leaves them on the clipboard for ⌘V.

entries.headline: Voice editing — “scratch that”, “delete last sentence”, “undo”
entries.body: Fix a misspoken phrase without deleting and re-dictating. A deterministic, offline command layer edits the in-progress text before it's committed. No AI required.

howTo.summary: In Preview mode, say the command on its own and it edits the pending text.
steps: Set Settings › Output › Delivery to “Preview, then insert” (the mode that holds the text on-screen until you release the key).
Leave “Spoken edit commands” on in that same Delivery section (it’s on by default).
Dictate as usual, then pause and say a command on its own — “scratch that” drops the last thing you said, “undo” brings it back.
Release the key: the edited text is what gets inserted.
say: “scratch that” — drop the last thing you said
howTo.note: Works in Preview mode (the text is held until release, so an edit can still change it). A command is recognized only when the WHOLE phrase is spoken on its own — say it as its own short utterance, with a pause, so the recognizer punctuates it as a separate sentence. A command buried inside a longer phrase (“finish the report scratch that let me redo”) is left as plain text on purpose, so ordinary speech like “scratch the surface” is never eaten. Parser is case- and punctuation-tolerant (including … and curly quotes).

entries.headline: A self-learning dictionary — star, sort by use, and accept corrections it proposes
entries.body: Your Substitutions list now sorts your starred and most-used rules to the top and shows how often each has fired. And when you fix a single misheard word right after dictating, OpenWhisp proposes that fix for you to accept into the dictionary — learned and stored entirely on your Mac, never uploaded.

howTo.summary: Star and reorder your rules by use, and accept the corrections OpenWhisp learns from your type-overs.
steps: Open Settings › Cleanup › Vocabulary. Your Substitutions open sorted starred-first then most-used, each with a 'used N×' count; 'Sort by use' re-sorts on demand (rows stay put while you type so nothing jumps under the cursor).
Click the star on any rule to keep it at the top on the next sort.
Dictate into a normal text field, then immediately type over a single misheard word to fix it (e.g. 'kubernetis' → 'kubernetes').
OpenWhisp adds that fix to 'Suggested corrections' at the top of the Vocabulary section — click Add to make it a rule, or Dismiss to never be offered it again.
Turn the whole capture off with 'Learn corrections as I type over them' if you don't want it.
howTo.note: Live today: star + usage sort + per-rule usage counts, and the full accept/dismiss flow — an accepted suggestion becomes a real substitution that rewrites future transcripts, and nothing is ever added silently. How a suggestion appears today: after an insert made via the Accessibility path, if you type over ONE word within a couple of seconds while the SAME field stays focused and its text is readable via Accessibility, that edit is captured and run through the conservative learner (single-word casing/spelling fixes only). Deferred: capture is a single short-delay re-read, not continuous observation — corrections you make after that window, in paste-only or some web/Electron fields (where the field text isn't Accessibility-readable), or that span multiple words, aren't captured yet. You can always add those rules by hand in the same list.

entries.headline: Richer local formatting — numbers, lists, and markdown
entries.body: Opt-in rules turn spoken structure into clean text: "bullet…" into a list, "twenty twenty-six" into 2026, "bold that" into markdown — all deterministic, all off by default so nothing surprises you.

howTo.summary: Turn on the rule groups you want in Settings, then just speak the structure.
steps: In Settings › Cleanup › Formatting, turn on the groups you want — Numbers and years, Currency, Spoken lists, Markdown commands. They're independent and off by default.
Dictate naturally — the rules rewrite structure locally, on-device, no LLM.
say: “twenty twenty six” → 2026  (spoken times like “ten thirty” are left alone)
howTo.note: Live now. Each group is off by default so it never touches ordinary prose until you turn it on.

entries.headline: Send dictations beyond the focused app
entries.body: Foundational plumbing for routing a transcript somewhere other than the app you're in — a file, a Shortcut, a webhook. Built to fail open: if a target can't take it, your text still lands where it always did. Never dropped.

howTo.summary: Route a dictation to a file, Shortcut, or webhook instead of the focused app.
steps: Open Settings › Output › Output target and pick a destination: Focused app (default), File, Shortcut, or Webhook.
Fill in that target's details (a file path, a Shortcut, or a webhook URL).
Dictate as usual — the final text goes to your chosen target. If it isn't configured or a delivery fails, your words still land in the focused app — never dropped.
howTo.note: Live now. The choice is global (one destination for all apps) for this version. Live-typing (“Type live as you speak”) always goes to the focused app; only the final transcript is routed.

entries.headline: Dictate straight into a Markdown or text file
entries.body: Point OpenWhisp at a file — an Obsidian daily note, a Logseq journal, a scratch .md — and your dictation gets appended there instead of typed into the focused app. Add a dated heading if you like, or overwrite for a rolling "last dictation" buffer. All local; if the file can't be written, your words still land in the focused app — never dropped.

howTo.summary: Choose File as the output target; each dictation is appended with an optional dated heading.
steps: Open Settings › Output › Output target and choose File, then Choose… the file to write to (any .md or .txt — e.g. your vault's daily note).
Optionally set a heading template with {{date}}, {{time}}, or {{datetime}} tokens (e.g. "## {{datetime}}") to stamp each entry.
Choose Append (add each dictation to the end, blank-line separated) or Overwrite (keep only the latest).
Dictate — the final text is written to the file; live partials are ignored so you get one clean entry.
howTo.note: Live now. All local; if the file can't be written, your words still land in the focused app — never dropped.

entries.headline: Send a dictation straight to a webhook (Notion, Obsidian, Zapier, n8n…)
entries.body: POST your finished transcript as JSON — text, language, app, and timestamp — to any URL you configure, with optional auth headers. If the endpoint is down or slow, your words still land in the focused app as usual. Never dropped.

howTo.summary: Point the output target at a URL; OpenWhisp POSTs each dictation there as JSON.
steps: Open Settings › Output › Output target and choose Webhook, then enter your URL and add any headers your endpoint needs (e.g. an Authorization token).
Dictate as usual — OpenWhisp POSTs { text, language, appBundleID, timestamp } as JSON to your URL.
If the POST fails (non-2xx, network error, or timeout), the same text is typed into the focused app instead — you never lose it.
howTo.note: Live now. Content-Type: application/json is always set; your custom headers are applied verbatim, with a short timeout so a slow endpoint fails open quickly.

entries.headline: Silence no longer errors on one backend but not the other
entries.body: Dictating nothing now quietly produces nothing on both whisper backends — no more stray error toast depending on which engine you'd picked in Advanced settings.

entries.headline: OpenWhisp can't accidentally kill your other whisper servers
entries.body: The engine now checks a process is one it actually launched — by full path, not just name — before signaling it, so your own Homebrew or hand-built whisper-server is safe. Plus a fix for a startup port race.

entries.headline: A data race in Apple Speech dictation, closed
entries.body: Session state is now confined to a single context, so a late recognition callback can never leak a partial from one dictation into the next.

entries.headline: Agent rate limiting counts sessions on one honest clock
entries.body: The per-client session cap could be bypassed by a long-running session straddling the window edge. It now measures membership and expiry on the same clock, so the cap holds.

entries.headline: Post-processing scripts clean up after themselves
entries.body: Timed-out post-processing scripts now reap reliably — honest about best-effort process-group isolation, with a guarded kill that can never signal OpenWhisp's own processes.

entries.headline: The audio-device watcher tears down cleanly
entries.body: The CoreAudio listener that notices when you plug in a mic now removes itself symmetrically — no lingering, unremovable observer.

entries.headline: One place for text transforms
entries.body: The dictation pipeline now runs through a single, ordered post-processing chain — the groundwork that lets new transforms and output targets drop in cleanly, with behavior verified byte-for-byte against the old path.

entries.headline: Corrupt settings files can't take the app down
entries.body: All five on-device data stores now share one hardened loader: a bad file is quarantined and the app carries on with sane defaults, instead of a fix living in only one of them.

entries.headline: End-to-end audio testing, so features stay working
entries.body: A full regression suite now feeds pre-recorded audio through the whole pipeline — the reason "983 tests passing" is more than a number. Every feature above ships with coverage.
